Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure:
  - Persistent dry cough and rhinorrhea for ~5–6 days. No specific trigger or exposure reported.
- Symptom timeline and progression:
  - Onset ~5–6 days ago; cough is continuous, dry, worse at night, wakes patient and causes sore throat from coughing. Initial brief diarrhea at onset resolved. Subjective chills/feeling feverish (no measured temperature). Generalized myalgias and marked fatigue; some improvement in GI symptoms but cough persists.
- ENT symptoms:
  - Throat: irritation/sore throat secondary to coughing; no odynophagia or pain with swallowing.
  - Voice/hoarseness: not reported.
  - Drooling: none.
  - Nasal/ocular: runny nose (rhinorrhea); no eye symptoms described.
  - Stridor/noisy breathing: none reported.
  - Dyspnea: none at baseline; transient breathlessness associated with coughing episodes only.
  - Distribution of swelling (lips/tongue/uvula/face): none reported.
  - Ear/neck: no ear pain, blockage, or discharge; no neck swelling or pain.
- Relevant past episodes and treatments:
  - No prior similar episodes or prior ED/hospital care for this complaint stated.
- Allergies and current medications:
  - Allergies: none reported.
  - Medications: Metformin — not documented (dose/route/frequency not documented); Lisinopril — not documented (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Relevant social context:
  - Lives with partner (partner currently well). Patient able to attend work some days but has taken at least one sick day; former smoker (stopped ~6 months ago). Alcohol: wine 2–3 glasses on ~3 evenings/week.

Objective:
- Observable swelling/distribution: none observed or reported.
- Airway/breathing descriptors:
  - No stridor or noisy breathing reported. Patient reports transient breathlessness only during severe coughing spells.
- Mental status and associated features:
  - Alert, oriented; reports fatigue, myalgias, shivering.
- Vitals and examination findings:
  - Not recorded.
- Other observations:
  - Clinician noted audible cough during the call.
- Presence of another person with the patient:
  - Not recorded (patient reports living with partner but presence during call not stated).

Assessment:
- Working clinical impression:
  - Most likely viral upper respiratory infection/acute bronchitis causing persistent dry cough and rhinorrhea; possible influenza or alternative contributors (see DDx).
- Brief evidence summary from transcript:
  - Dry, continuous cough for 5–6 days with nocturnal worsening, associated rhinorrhea, subjective chills/fever, myalgias, transient diarrhea at onset, and generalized lethargy; no focal chest pain, no baseline dyspnea, no ear/neck complaints.
- Differential diagnosis (top 2–3 from provided DDx consistent with transcript):
  1. Viral upper respiratory infection / acute bronchitis — High likelihood.
     - Justification: Onset ~5–6 days with runny nose, continuous dry cough worse at night, myalgias and subjective fever/chills consistent with viral prodrome.
     - Opposing evidence: No objectively recorded temperature; cough has persisted nearly a week — reconsider if no improvement.
  2. Influenza — Medium likelihood.
     - Justification: Prominent systemic symptoms (shivers/chills, marked myalgias, fatigue) with acute cough and rhinorrhea can reflect influenza.
     - Opposing evidence: No documented high fever or abrupt, severe onset; partner asymptomatic.
  3. ACE inhibitor–induced cough (lisinopril) — Medium likelihood (consider if cough persists).
     - Justification: Lisinopril is associated with a dry, nocturnal cough; patient is taking lisinopril.
     - Opposing evidence: Temporal association with systemic viral symptoms (feverishness, myalgias, transient diarrhea) suggests infectious etiology; ACEI cough typically develops over weeks–months rather than acutely.

Plan:
- Immediate actions taken/advised (per visit):
  - Symptomatic measures advised: rest, maintain hydration, regular paracetamol for symptomatic relief.
  - Patient advised to consider taking 1–2 days off work while symptomatic to rest and reduce potential transmissibility.
  - Return/seek earlier review if symptoms worsen.
- Specific patient/caregiver instructions:
  - Monitor symptoms at home; seek earlier medical review if any of the following occur: increasing shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, noisy breathing/stridor, chest pain, high or persistent fever, inability to maintain oral intake, worsening mental status, or hemoptysis.
  - If cough and systemic symptoms do not improve in 2–3 days, re-evaluation recommended (possible assessment for secondary bacterial infection and consideration of antibiotics).
  - If cough persists beyond expected course, discuss medication review with primary care regarding lisinopril as a possible contributor.
- Escalation criteria / red flags:
  - New or worsening dyspnea, voice change/hoarseness, throat closing sensation, stridor, persistent high fever, chest pain, syncope, or severe deterioration — seek urgent care/ED.
- Follow-up:
  - Reassess in 2–3 days if no improvement, earlier if red flags develop.
  - Consider primary care or ENT/allergy referral if cough persists beyond expected post-viral period or if alternative causes (ACE inhibitor cough, asthma/reactive airways, COVID-19) need formal evaluation.
  - COVID-19 testing not discussed in the transcript; patient to consider testing per local guidance or if clinically indicated on re-evaluation.
- Other considerations from DDx consistent with transcript:
  - If symptoms are consistent with influenza season and severity warrants, consider influenza testing and antiviral therapy per local protocols (not discussed in visit; follow-up assessment required).

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Objective vital signs (temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation) not recorded.
  - Physical examination (chest auscultation) and pulse oximetry not performed/documented.
  - No COVID-19 testing status recorded.
  - No documentation of prior similar cough episodes or prior evaluation for ACE inhibitor cough.
  - Medication doses/frequencies not documented for Metformin and Lisinopril.
  - No pregnancy status documented (if relevant).
  - No allergy or anaphylaxis action plan needed (patient reports no allergies).
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  - None identified; DDx aligns with transcript. (If any differing emphasis: DDx highlights ACE inhibitor cough as a possible contributor — transcript did not raise this, but it is consistent with medication history.)
- Transcript quality:
  - Audio/dialogue intelligible with minor hesitations; clinician heard audible cough on the call. Overall sufficient for telephonic assessment though lacking objective vitals/exam.
